about: code-server is an open-source project that runs VS Code on a server and opens it in any browser, a self-hosted alternative to GitHub Codespaces. You get the editor, its terminal and your extensions on a laptop or an iPad, with the same setup on each. Tests, builds and downloads run on the server, so the device in your hands keeps its battery.

People run code-server for one development environment that follows them, on a server they choose, free under the MIT license. Settings are kept on the server's disk, as in desktop VS Code, and its web views do not call out to Microsoft's servers. The catch is that Microsoft's closed-source extensions, Live Share and the Remote ones for SSH, Containers and WSL, do not work.

faq.q: Is code-server free and open source?
faq.a: Yes. code-server is free under the MIT license, and its source is on GitHub at coder/code-server, a project of Coder.

faq.q: What is the difference between code-server and GitHub Codespaces?
faq.a: Both open VS Code in a browser. Codespaces is a closed-source, paid service from GitHub and Microsoft; code-server is free software on your own server, with password sign-in, a built-in proxy to the server's ports and your choice of marketplace.

faq.q: Does code-server support VS Code extensions?
faq.a: Yes, from the Open VSX gallery rather than Microsoft's marketplace, whose terms limit it to Microsoft's products. You can also install a .vsix file, or point code-server at another marketplace with $EXTENSIONS_GALLERY.

faq.q: Can I use code-server on an iPad?
faq.a: Yes. Open it in Safari, tap Share, then Add to Home Screen: as an app it gets more room and shortcuts such as cmd+w. Expect to edit some shortcuts, and ctrl+c does not stop a long-running terminal process.

faq.q: Can several people share one code-server?
faq.a: Not well. code-server was built for individuals, with a single password. For several users the project recommends one virtual machine each, and it points teams to Coder, made by the same company.
